outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20 and further strikes reported on subsequent days, including overnight and on the morning of Wednesday, Nov 25, and additional Wednesday afternoon strikes in several regions. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, and later Wednesday by Al Jazeera, said Russia had again attacked energy facilities overnight and on Wednesday morning, targeting power plants and electricity transmission and distribution substations, and that the attacks caused new power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25 report, quoted Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov as saying the situation was difficult in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk, where the attacks damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, said a significant number of energy facilities important to regional electricity supply had been damaged over the past day, that the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region. The Energy Ministry, as reported by the same Wednesday morning accounts, and the IAEA, as reported by TASS citing an IAEA press-service statement, said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators. Later Wednesday accounts described further regional damage, including another attack on main power grids in Dnipropetrovsk region, a renewed outage in Zaporizhzhia region after a partial restoration, an afternoon strike-drone attack that cut power in parts of two Odesa city districts, and a Shahed-type UAV attack that left 85 settlements in Mykolaiv district without electricity before the regional administration later said those customers had been re-energized. Ukrenergo, as reported Wednesday evening by Apostrophe at 9:23 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, and by 24 Kanal, said that on Thursday, Nov 26, stabilization measures would be in effect around the clock in a number of regions because of the consequences of strikes on energy-infrastructure facilities: hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for household consumers, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and that exact times should be checked on the official pages of the local distribution-system operator, with the volume of restrictions possibly adjusted during the day. Earlier Tuesday evening accounts, including UNN, kurs.com.ua, 24tv.ua, and UNIAN, citing Ukrenergo, had already said planned outage schedules would be in effect around the clock on Wednesday, Nov 25, in parts of the country, with hourly outages of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), said that as of Wednesday morning, as a result of Russian attacks over the past day that damaged a significant number of energy facilities important to regional electricity supply, there were de-energized consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. The same report said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, and that emergency outages were in effect in Dnipropetrovsk region, with restoration work continuing. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform, also said that because of damage to energy equipment, restrictions would be in effect until the end of the day in some regions: capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, and that current schedules should be checked on the official pages of the distribution-system operator. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine at 11:49 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:49 a.m. CT), by Ukrainska Pravda at 10:42 a.m. Wednesday (2:42 a.m. CT), and by UNN at 8:35 a.m. Wednesday (12:35 a.m. CT), said Russia had again attacked energy facilities overnight and on Wednesday morning, targeting power plants and electricity transmission and distribution substations, and that the attacks caused new power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions. Those reports, citing the ministry, said repair and restoration work was ongoing in all affected regions, but that repeated attacks and constant air-raid alerts were significantly complicating the work and delaying restoration; that as of Wednesday morning the situation remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions; and that additional grid restrictions were being applied to prevent emergencies caused by equipment overload. Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25 report, likewise cited Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov on outages in those five regions and on a difficult situation in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk. The same Energy Ministry accounts, UNN citing the IAEA, and TASS, citing an IAEA press-service statement, said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators, the plant's 17th loss of external power since the beginning of 2026 and, according to the IAEA as reported by TASS and earlier by UNN, the 28th complete loss of off-site power during the conflict. The IAEA, as quoted by TASS, said the outage occurred at 5:28 a.m. local time after the plant lost connection to its last operating external power line, Ferosplavna-1, and that IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said the agency's team at the site was investigating the cause and location of the line outage. Later Wednesday regional reports, detailed in the rows below, described further afternoon damage and outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Odesa, and a Shahed-type UAV attack that, according to Heorhii Reshetilov of the Mykolaiv regional military administration as reported by Interfax-Ukraine at 3:31 p.m. Wednesday (7:31 a.m. CT) and Ukrinform at 3:41 p.m. Wednesday (7:41 a.m. CT), left 85 settlements in Mykolaiv district without electricity; Suspilne, in a 6:38 p.m. Wednesday (10:38 a.m. CT) update citing the regional administration, said all consumers left without electricity after that Wednesday attack had already been re-energized. An earlier Tuesday evening Ukrenergo statement, as reported by UNN at 5:02 p.m. Tuesday, Nov 24 (9:02 a.m. CT), by kurs.com.ua, and by 24tv.ua, and by UNIAN, had already said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, planned outages would again be in effect around the clock in parts of the country, with hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, corresponding to about two to 12 hours without electricity, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. Ukrenergo, as reported by Apostrophe at 9:23 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (1:23 p.m. CT), and by 24 Kanal, said that on Thursday, Nov 26, stabilization measures would be in effect throughout the day in a number of regions because of the consequences of strikes on energy-infrastructure facilities, with hourly outage schedules of 0.5 to 3.5 queues for household consumers and capacity-limitation schedules for industry, and that consumers should check current schedules for a given address on the official resources of the local distribution-system operator. Apostrophe's Wednesday evening report, citing Ukrenergo, also recapped that Russian shelling on the morning of Nov 25 had caused outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, and Kharkiv regions, that the most difficult situation remained in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia energy workers had been able to partially re-energize customers, and that emergency outages had been introduced in Dnipropetrovsk region, with repair crews continuing emergency restoration work. No later official confirmation was found that external power at the occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, which the Energy Ministry and IAEA said was lost on Wednesday morning after the Ferosplavna-1 line went out, had been restored. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, EET).

outages.place: Odesa, including Prymorskyi and Peresypskyi districts, and parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20, further damage reported over Nov 24-25, and a massive strike-drone attack on Odesa and its suburbs on the afternoon of Wednesday, Nov 25. Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region. Kiper, as reported later Wednesday by Censor.NET at 1:59 p.m. and by Kyiv Post, said Russian forces had launched a massive attack with strike drones against Odesa and its suburbs, targeting civilian and energy infrastructure. DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, as reported Wednesday morning by Odessa Life in an update at 7:54 a.m., said stabilization outages would be applied in Odesa and Odesa region on Wednesday, Nov 25, on Ukrenergo's command, and that schedules could be adjusted if Ukrenergo's commands changed. The same Odessa Life report, citing the company, also said urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district would leave that area without electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Wednesday, as previously announced
outages.affected: Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform at 12:43 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (4:43 a.m. CT), said that over the past day Russian attacks had again damaged energy equipment in Odesa region, and that about 9,000 subscribers in parts of Odesa and Bolhrad districts of the region were temporarily without electricity. Kiper, as reported by Ukrinform, also said that during the previous evening's attack a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi production site in the region had been damaged, including 16 units of special-purpose vehicles, and that company employees were not injured. Later on Wednesday, Kiper, as reported by Censor.NET at 1:59 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (5:59 a.m. CT), and by Kyiv Post in a report dated 3:53 p.m. Wednesday (7:53 a.m. CT), said Russian forces had launched a massive strike-drone attack on Odesa and its suburbs, damaging a residential complex, a private logistics facility, and a plant making paper-based household products, and that some consumers in Odesa's Peresypskyi and Prymorskyi districts had been left without electricity. Those accounts, citing Kiper, said critical-infrastructure facilities were being switched to backup power, that medical institutions continued operating without disruptions, and that energy workers were working to restore electricity supply. Censor.NET, citing DTEK, also said some critical-infrastructure facilities were operating with interruptions. Kyiv Post said Odesa city military administration head Serhiy Lysak first reported the attack in a Telegram post at 12:10 p.m. Wednesday (4:10 a.m. CT) and later said three people had been injured. No official customer count was found for the Wednesday afternoon outage in the Prymorskyi and Peresypskyi districts. Odessa Life, in a Wednesday report published at 6:42 a.m. and updated at 7:54 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (10:42 p.m. and 11:54 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24), citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said that on Wednesday, Nov 25, stabilization outages would be in effect in Odesa and Odesa region on Ukrenergo's command, that residents should check the schedule for a given address on the company's website, Viber group, or Telegram chatbot, and that if Ukrenergo's commands changed the schedules could also be adjusted. The same report said energy workers would carry out urgent equipment repairs in Odesa's Peresypskyi district, where there would be no electricity from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy and Ukrenergo, in Wednesday morning updates reported by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, UNN, and Ukrinform, listed Odesa region among five regions with new power outages after overnight and Wednesday-morning attacks. Odessa Life, in a report published at 7:17 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (11:17 p.m. CT Wednesday, Nov 25), citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said that on Thursday, Nov 26, stabilization outages in Odesa and Odesa region would apply to all 12 of the company's schedule groups because of the consequences of attacks on the energy system, that the schedule had been updated at 7:01 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, and that if Ukrenergo's commands changed the schedules could also be adjusted. The same report said residents should check a given address on the company's website, Viber group, or Telegram chatbot. No official combined customer count for outages in the city and region was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, EET).

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, including strikes on Nov 24 and overnight into Nov 25, a Wednesday, Nov 25, attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, and a later Wednesday attack that DTEK said damaged main power grids. DTEK, as reported Wednesday morning by UNN and by 5692.com.ua, said a massive Wednesday attack had stopped generation at one of the company's thermal power plants, had significantly damaged equipment, and was the company's third massive plant attack in November alone, and that because of the strikes, homes and part of critical infrastructure were left without electricity, with emergency outages by Ukrenergo order in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, where schedules were not in effect. Ukrainska Pravda, in a report time-stamped 5:31 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, citing DTEK, and RBC-Ukraine, in a report time-stamped 4:30 p.m. Wednesday, also citing DTEK's official Telegram channel, said another Russian attack had damaged main power grids and again left parts of Dnipro and the same four districts without electricity
outages.affected: DTEK, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda at 5:31 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (9:31 a.m. CT), and by RBC-Ukraine at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday (8:30 a.m. CT), citing DTEK's official Telegram channel, said that after another Russian attack, main power grids had been damaged and that parts of Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts were without electricity. Those reports, citing DTEK, said energy workers would begin restoration work as soon as the security situation allowed, and that electricity would first be restored to critical-infrastructure facilities. DTEK, as reported earlier by UNN at 9:51 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (1:51 a.m. CT), said that on Wednesday Russia had carried out a massive attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, that the plant had stopped generating electricity, that equipment had been significantly damaged, and that this was already the third massive attack on the company's plants in November alone. The same DTEK statement, as reported by UNN and by 5692.com.ua in a report time-stamped 11:22 a.m. Wednesday (3:22 a.m. CT) on a DTEK update as of 10:26 a.m. Wednesday (2:26 a.m. CT), said that on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday Russia had again struck energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, and that because of those strikes homes and part of critical infrastructure were left without electricity. DTEK said that by order of Ukrenergo, emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, and that hourly schedules were not in effect there, so a restoration time could not be determined from the usual schedule. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy and Ukrenergo, in Wednesday morning updates, described the situation in Dnipropetrovsk region as especially difficult. Informator, citing a Ukrenergo publication, said that on Thursday, Nov 26, hourly outage schedules would be in effect around the clock, from 12:00 a.m. to 11:59 p.m., in Dnipropetrovsk region, with 0.5 to 3.5 queues of consumers to be disconnected at a time across Ukraine, and with capacity limits for industry, and that current schedules should be checked on the official pages of the local distribution-system operator. The same Informator report published approximate Thursday group times for DTEK subscribers if emergency outages were not in effect in Dnipro and the region. No later official DTEK confirmation was found that the Wednesday emergency outages in Dnipro and the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts had ended. No official customer count was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, EET).

outages.cause: Damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, according to JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo, including a further Wednesday attack that again cut power to some consumers after a partial restoration. The company's head, Andriy Stasevsky, in a Wednesday morning statement reported by Interfax-Ukraine, said a significant number of consumers in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity as a result of that damage, and that the emergency response plan for systemic power-grid failures had been activated. Later Wednesday, Zaporizhzhia regional military administration head Mykhailo Semikin, as reported by Ekonomichna Pravda at 4:24 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25, said the enemy had again damaged the region's energy infrastructure, and that people who had already had electricity restored after the mass outage were again without power. Stasevsky, in the same Ekonomichna Pravda report, said some consumers who had been re-energized after the mass outage were again without electricity, and that work to restore supply was continuing. Ukraine's Ministry of Energy, as reported Wednesday morning by Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda, and UNN, said the situation as of Wednesday morning remained most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where attacks had damaged a significant number of energy facilities essential to electricity supply
outages.affected: Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, as reported by Ekonomichna Pravda at 4:24 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (8:24 a.m. CT), said a further Russian attack had again damaged the region's energy infrastructure, and that people who had already had electricity restored after the mass outage were again without power. Andriy Stasevsky, head of JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo, as quoted in the same Ekonomichna Pravda report, said some consumers who had been re-energized after the mass outage were again without electricity, and that the company was continuing work to restore supply. Those later accounts did not give a customer count. Earlier Wednesday, Stasevsky, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine in Ukrainian at 7:36 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:36 p.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24) and in English at 9:21 a.m. Wednesday (1:21 a.m. CT), said that as a result of damage to energy infrastructure caused by shelling by Russian occupation forces, a significant number of consumers in the city of Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity, that the emergency response plan for systemic power-grid failures had been activated, and that the company was working to restore electricity supply. Censor.NET, in a report time-stamped 7:12 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (11:12 p.m. CT Tuesday), citing Semikin, likewise said that because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, part of the residents of Zaporizhzhia region had been left without electricity, and quoted the same morning Stasevsky statement. Ukrenergo, as reported by Ukrinform at 11:06 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (3:06 a.m. CT), said the situation remained especially difficult in Dnipropetrovsk region and Zaporizhzhia region, and that after large-scale outages in Zaporizhzhia electricity supply had been partially restored, with restoration work continuing. Inform.zp.ua, in a report published at 10:12 a.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:12 a.m. CT), citing Zaporizhiaoblenergo, said hourly outage schedules for Zaporizhzhia and the region on Nov 25 had been updated on Ukrenergo's instructions, with the schedule updated at 7:21 a.m. Wednesday (11:21 p.m. CT Tuesday). Inform.zp.ua, in a report published at 7:06 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (11:06 p.m. CT Wednesday, Nov 25), citing JSC Zaporizhiaoblenergo, said hourly outage schedules for Zaporizhzhia and Zaporizhzhia region on Thursday, Nov 26, had been updated, and published group times that included, with 30 minutes allowed for switching, outages such as 12:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m., 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., and 5:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. for queue 1.1, and said schedules could change during the day depending on the situation in Ukraine's power system. No official customer count was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, EET).

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: The New Region, in a Nov 23, 2026 report, said gas production at the Khor Mor field was expected to resume in the coming days after a Monday meeting of delegations from Erbil and Baghdad with the field's operator, Dana Gas; that, according to information acquired by The New Region, the outcome of the meeting was positive, with Dana Gas set to resume gas production in the next two to three days; and that a source at the field told The New Region that all employees at Khor Mor had returned to work, that Dana Gas was set to release a statement on the resumption of operations in the near future, that efforts to repair the damaged sections were also expected to begin soon, and that production was expected to resume within the next 48 hours in areas unaffected by the attack. Omed Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry, told The New Region on Monday that electricity generation at power stations was expected to resume within hours of gas production restarting, with supply gradually increasing, but that it could take up to 24 hours of normal operations for electricity production to return to pre-attack levels. Those reports did not say that Khor Mor production or pre-attack electricity supply had already resumed. An earlier Nov 22, 2026 report by The New Region had said the Monday meeting was planned to discuss resuming production, that Dana Gas was expected to insist on security guarantees against further attacks, and that if an agreement were reached on Monday, a specialized Turkish company would begin repairs estimated to take six days. Kurdistan24, in a Nov 22, 2026 report, said the Nov 8 drone attack in Sulaimani province caused a large fire and stopped gas production entirely, with no casualties, and that the stoppage cut 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts of electricity in the Kurdistan Region and reduced power-supply hours by five to six hours a day. That account is consistent with earlier official figures: Al Jazeera, on Nov 9, citing Iraqi and Kurdish officials and the official Iraqi News Agency, said the attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power and, citing Omed Ahmed, that it suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal, and Duhok and knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts off the grid. Rudaw later quoted Ahmed as saying authorities had increased generation from approximately 1,000 megawatts immediately after the attack to 1,550 megawatts, of which 50 megawatts were reserved for essential facilities and factories, leaving 1,500 megawatts for residents and raising daily public electricity supply to six to eight hours; Ahmed said the electricity then available covered only 40 percent of demand, leaving a 60 percent shortfall, and that no date had been established for production to resume. Rudaw's article image assets for that report are dated Nov 13, 2026. 964media, in a Nov 15 report, quoted Ahmed as saying that no timeframe had been set for supplies to return to normal and that within 48 hours of the attack generation had been increased from 1,000 megawatts to nearly 1,650 megawatts. Dana Gas, in a Nov 14 clarification later restated in coverage including a Kurdistan24 report, said the facility had sustained significant damage and that no gas could currently be produced. The Insight International, in a Nov 21 report citing private-generator officials who spoke to Rudaw on Saturday, Nov 21, said the public grid remained weak because of the gas shortfall and that neighborhood generators were still running for most of the day in Erbil, Sulaimani, and Duhok. No official customer count was given. No later official confirmation that Khor Mor production had already resumed was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (9:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Iraq time), about two to three days after the Monday, Nov 23, meeting described in The New Region's Nov 23 report.

outages.cause: An attack on transmission infrastructure in southwestern Colombia on the afternoon of Nov 24, 2026, according to Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy, in a Nov 25 statement that said the attack had occurred the previous afternoon, and according to XM, the operator of the National Interconnected System. XM, in a Nov 25 update, also said that before this event the system had already been operating with a degraded network because of attacks a week earlier, leaving fewer options to serve demand in Caquetá, Putumayo, southern Huila, Cauca, and Nariño.
outages.affected: XM, the operator of Colombia's National Interconnected System, in an official update dated Nov 25, 2026, said that as a consequence of the Nov 24 transmission-network event in the country's southwest, affectations persisted in serving demand in Cauca, Nariño, Putumayo, Caquetá, and southern Huila, and that restoration was advancing according to operating conditions, with demand-serving capacity in the affected zone limited because the system had already been operating with a degraded network after attacks a week earlier. XM said that as of 6:00 p.m. Colombia time Wednesday, Nov 25 (5:00 p.m. CT), demand served, measured as power in megawatts against forecast demand in each zone and not as a share of customers or households with service, was 188 MW of 332 MW forecast in Cauca and Nariño (57%), 19.2 MW of 37 MW in Putumayo (52%), 28 MW of 69 MW in southern Huila (41%), and 24 MW of 60 MW in Caquetá (40%), according to those 6:00 p.m. figures as reported by BluRadio, citing XM. XM's own 6:00 p.m. update said the percentages correspond to power served versus forecast demand at the cutoff time, that the figures vary with restoration maneuvers, and that forecast demand is updated between communiqués, so a change in the percentage does not always mean less energy delivered. XM also said further interruptions were possible because of reduced availability of national and regional transmission circuits, and that it was not possible to set an exact time for normalization, because restoration depends on the actions the affected companies can take to recover and return the infrastructure to service. Earlier Wednesday, Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy, in a statement dated Nov 25, said that after an attack on electrical infrastructure the previous afternoon, the electrical system was serving about 68% of energy demand in the country's southwest, and it gave these morning figures: Putumayo 72%, Cauca and Nariño 71%, southern Huila 69%, and Caquetá 48%, which it called the most affected department. An earlier XM official update as of 11:30 a.m. Colombia time Wednesday, Nov 25 (10:30 a.m. CT), had given departmental demand served of 164 MW of 246 MW forecast in Cauca and Nariño (66.7%), 7 MW of 32 MW in Putumayo (21.9%), 21 MW of 56 MW in Caquetá (37.5%), and 31 MW of 64 MW in southern Huila (48.4%). Diario del Sur, in a report dated 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, Nov 25 (2:30 p.m. CT), said Electrocaquetá had partially restored service with 20 megawatts, and quoted distribution manager Jaime Zapata Franco as saying electricity was then available in Florencia, El Doncello, and part of Morelia, while the department's other municipalities remained without service, and that if available capacity stayed at 20 megawatts overnight, a rotation of supply was not ruled out. No official customer count was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (1:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Colombia time).

outages.cause: A collapse of transmission tower T313 in Ranau early Thursday morning, Nov 26, 2026, which Sabah Electricity, in a Thursday statement reported by Sinar Harian, said affected both circuits of the transmission line and caused a power disruption to Sabah's east coast. The company said the incident was detected at 6:04 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time, and that technical teams were carrying out a comprehensive assessment at the site to identify the cause and determine the fastest, most effective, and safest restoration method. The Star, in a Thursday report, said Sabah Electricity had reported an incident on its electricity transmission system at 6:04 a.m. that caused the outage, and that photographs circulating on social media showed a collapsed transmission tower and power lines obstructing the main Ranau-Sandakan road. Malay Mail, citing Sabah Electricity, likewise said an incident on the transmission system at 6:04 a.m. caused a power outage affecting the East Coast
outages.affected: Sabah Electricity, as reported by Sinar Harian at 1:19 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time (11:19 p.m. CT Wednesday, Nov 25), and by The Star at 12:40 p.m. Thursday (10:40 p.m. CT Wednesday), said eight east-coast districts were affected: Sandakan, Tawau, Lahad Datu, Semporna, Kunak, Beluran, Telupid, and Kinabatangan. The company said technical teams were carrying out a comprehensive assessment at the site, that mobile generator sets were on the way to affected areas as an alternative measure to help restore supply, and that all available resources, assets, and manpower were being mobilized, with priority on accelerating restoration without compromising safety. The Star said Sabah Electricity had not given a number of consumers affected or said when electricity supply would be fully restored, and that restoration works were ongoing, with priority given to works at the site without compromising public safety. outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike; he said affected areas continued to experience prolonged outages and scheduled power cuts as of this week. The report said the Sudan Electricity Holding Company and Ministry of Energy had yet to publicly announce the restoration of the major facilities damaged in the attacks. A United Nations report published Nov 17, issued in Geneva and posted on the UN in Sudan website, said that in just over two weeks between Oct 20 and Nov 4, 29 drone strikes, attributed to the Rapid Support Forces, hit electricity facilities and fuel stations across 11 states, triggering widespread power blackouts and further fuel shortages affecting millions far from the conflict frontlines. An earlier Al Jazeera Nov 15 feature said there is no clear schedule for the resulting power cuts, which can last anywhere between six hours and a day, and, citing The Associated Press, said repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100 MW. Residents and a small-business owner in Port Sudan described prolonged, unreliable cuts, including outages lasting more than 24 hours. Al-Ghad Al-Sudani, in a report last updated Nov 22, 2026, said explosions and drone flights returned to Khartoum on Sunday morning, Nov 22, amid reports of attacks on military sites in various parts of the capital, and that the attacks coincided with power outages in large parts of the city; the report did not give a customer count or independently establish the cause of that outage. Democracy Now, in a Nov 24, 2026 headline, said Sudan's military reported intercepting drones launched by the Rapid Support Forces over Khartoum after attacks that struck the city's main airport and several buildings, including a U.N. facility, and that those attacks came as Sudan's power grid was on the brink of collapse following attacks on electricity stations; that headline did not state that the Nov 24 drone activity itself had struck power stations or give a customer count. No later official national customer count or official restoration timetable was found as of 12:00 AM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (8:00 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Sudan time).
